clue.text: Tractor crushed crate with pole

indicators.note: something crushed is squashed out of its shape, so the word before it loses its letter order

blocks.note: the word to be rearranged
a pillar is an upright post

explanation.surface: A farm vehicle has run over a wooden box and a post.
explanation.walkthrough: Caterpillar is the trade name for a tracked tractor, so the definition is fair even with no insect in sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Caterpillar is a brand of heavy tracked vehicle, and the name is used generically for tracked tractors.

clue.text: Like Luke xii.9? Exactly!

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase for a phrase-noun

blocks.note: first meaning: a Bible reference given by book number and verse number
second meaning: with precise detail, as in quoting a source

explanation.walkthrough: Luke xii.9 is chapter twelve, verse nine of Luke's Gospel; giving that is citing the exact source.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the two numbers of a scripture citation and, as an idiom, means in full precise detail.

clue.text: Savour the start of surrealism in the Tate

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter only
in means placed inside, so one piece sits within the gallery's name

blocks.note: the Tate is a London art gallery; only its name is used
the opening letter of the art movement

explanation.surface: Enjoy an introduction to surrealist art at the Tate gallery in London.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tate is the London art gallery, but here only its name supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To taste something is to sample its flavour, and to savour it is to enjoy that flavour.

clue.text: Being uneasy, I've to take a breather first

definitions.note: a participle phrase for an adjective

indicators.note: first tells you which piece comes at the front, overriding the order the words are printed in

blocks.note: taking a breather means resting
the contraction with its apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A restless person says they need a pause before going on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' tells you the rest comes before I've, though the clue prints them the other way round.
explanation.definitionFit: Restive means fidgety and unable to keep still, an uneasy state of agitation.

clue.text: It's complete in itself, for example, in Bury

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another

blocks.note: to inter is to bury
e.g. abbreviates for example

explanation.surface: It looks like a remark about the self-contained town of Bury in Lancashire.
explanation.walkthrough: Bury is capitalised to look like the Lancashire town; it is the verb. INTER holds EG to give INTEGER.
explanation.definitionFit: Integer comes from the Latin for whole or untouched: a whole number with no fractional part.

clue.text: Reminisce and try to identify the stalker?

definitions.note: a whimsical phrase for the literal act

blocks.note: first meaning: recall past times
second meaning: turn your head to see who is following

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful literal reading: someone on your tail is behind you.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means remembering the past, and literally means turning round to see what is behind.

clue.text: Standing immobile, fix teeth to doorpost

indicators.note: to fix something can mean to rig or doctor it, so the letters are tampered with

blocks.note: the fifteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A dentist's grotesque method of keeping teeth in place by tying them to a doorpost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fix teeth' looks like dentistry, recalling the old string-and-door tooth extraction trick, but fix is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Being rooted to the spot is an idiom for being unable to move, frozen through fear or shock.

clue.text: Special day for prosperous union

blocks.note: golden can mean flourishing, as in a golden age
a wedding is a union of two people

explanation.surface: A wealthy couple's marriage day is a big celebration.
explanation.definitionFit: A golden wedding is the fiftieth anniversary of a marriage, a notable occasion celebrated by the couple.

clue.text: Famous 19th century soldier used common to go on round road

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so one word goes about the abbreviation

blocks.note: general means widespread or common
taken as written
taken as written
RD is the abbreviation for road

explanation.surface: A noted Victorian soldier marched along an ordinary ring road.
explanation.walkthrough: Gordon was the British general killed at Khartoum in 1885. Only 'on' goes round the road; 'go' sits outside before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Gordon was a celebrated British army officer of the Victorian era, killed defending Khartoum.

clue.text: On a steamship lives a famous shipowner

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
SS is the standard abbreviation for steamship
to live is to be, so lives gives is

explanation.surface: A wealthy magnate lives aboard one of his own steamers.
explanation.walkthrough: Aristotle Onassis was the Greek shipping tycoon who married Jacqueline Kennedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Aristotle Onassis built one of the largest private merchant fleets of the twentieth century.

clue.text: Couple to read book, which includes "Return of Miss Piggy"

indicators.note: a return goes back the way it came, so the word for the pig is read from its end
a thing that includes another holds it inside itself

blocks.note: a tome is a large book
a female pig is a sow

explanation.surface: A pair settle down with a book featuring the sequel adventures of the Muppet diva.
explanation.walkthrough: Miss Piggy is not a name to look up: a miss who is a piggy is a female pig. TOME holds WOS to give TWOSOME.
explanation.definitionFit: A twosome is a pair of people together, the same thing as a couple.

clue.text: I''m indecisive, so I'd better turn to the phone

definitions.note: the definition includes the speaker: the answer is what I am, not I'm

indicators.note: to turn round is to face the other way, so the two letters of the contraction are read backwards

blocks.note: the contraction with its apostrophe dropped
taken as written
to give someone a ring is to phone them

explanation.surface: Someone who cannot make up their mind decides to settle it by making a call.
explanation.walkthrough: DI, then THE, then RING. The clue's doubled apostrophe in I''m is a typo in the source.
explanation.definitionFit: Dithering means hesitating and failing to make up one's mind, which is what an indecisive person does.

clue.text: Note from brother's first girl

blocks.note: BR is an abbreviation for brother; the 's joins it to the next piece
in Genesis Eve is the first woman

explanation.surface: A letter arrives from a sibling's earliest girlfriend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' looks like a written message, but it is a musical note.
explanation.definitionFit: A breve is a long musical note, worth two semibreves in modern notation.

clue.text: Bellini's unfinished opera is standard

indicators.note: something unfinished stops short of its end, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: the possessive just says whose opera it is
Norma is Bellini's best-known opera

explanation.surface: A critic dismisses an incomplete Bellini opera as merely average.
explanation.definitionFit: A norm is the usual or expected level, a standard against which things are measured.

clue.text: Reformed tart to care for earthenware object

indicators.note: to be reformed is to be formed again in a new way, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the ten letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A former woman of loose morals now looks after a clay pot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reformed tart' paints a reformed character, but tart here is just letters to shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Terracotta is unglazed brownish-red fired clay, and a piece made from it can be called a terracotta.

clue.text: Photo shows train nearly in the harbour

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the last letter is cut off
in places the shortened word inside the harbour word

blocks.note: a port is a harbour
the word without its final letter

explanation.surface: A picture captures a train arriving at the docks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Photo' and 'train' suggest a railway snapshot; the harbour is the outer word, not the setting.
explanation.definitionFit: A portrait is a picture of a person, and a photograph of someone's face can be called one.

clue.text: Irish novelist to rewrite "Dinner with a Bone"

indicators.note: to rewrite something is to set it down again differently, so the letters are put in a new order

blocks.note: the word as printed has a second N the parse cannot use: the setter's slip
taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: An author is asked to revise a story titled Dinner with a Bone.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder as printed has one N too many: DINNER A BONE gives eleven letters for a ten-letter answer, so the setter presumably meant DINER.
explanation.definitionFit: Edna O'Brien was an Irish writer whose first book was The Country Girls.

clue.text: This ballet is right to include "Amber"

indicators.note: to include something is to take it in, so the colour sits inside

blocks.note: RT is an abbreviation for right
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dance company is correct to stage a piece called Amber.
explanation.walkthrough: Rambert is the oldest British dance company, founded by Marie Rambert.
explanation.definitionFit: Rambert, formerly Ballet Rambert, is a London-based dance company, so it is a ballet in the company sense.

clue.text: Pain for each Biblical woman losing a student

indicators.note: losing something means going without it, so a letter is dropped

blocks.note: ea is the abbreviation for each
Rachel was the wife of Jacob in Genesis
L for learner, a student

explanation.surface: Each woman from the Bible feels pain when one of her pupils leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: L stands for learner, as on British L-plates, and so for a student.
explanation.definitionFit: Earache is a specific kind of pain felt inside the ear.

clue.text: Speculator with a shilling ticket

blocks.note: s was the abbreviation for a shilling in old British money
a tag is a label or ticket attached to goods

explanation.surface: A gambler buys a ticket for a shilling, a former British coin worth five pence.
explanation.walkthrough: A stag in Stock Exchange slang buys newly issued shares hoping to sell them quickly at a profit.
explanation.definitionFit: Stock market slang calls someone who applies for new share issues to resell them at once a stag.

clue.text: A couple singing about victory will keep you warm

definitions.note: a clause describing the thing rather than a noun

indicators.note: about here means around, so one piece is wrapped round the other

blocks.note: a duet is a song for two performers
V is the abbreviation for victory, as in V-sign

explanation.surface: Two people singing a victory song keep their audience warm.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole tail of the clue is the definition, describing what a duvet does.
explanation.definitionFit: A duvet is a thick quilt filled with down or fibre used as bedding for warmth.

clue.text: Indication about Peg as a trader

indicators.note: about here means surrounding, so the first word goes round the second

blocks.note: a marker is a sign that indicates something
in golf the ball sits on a small peg called a tee

explanation.surface: A sign on a tent peg shows that someone is in business.
explanation.walkthrough: The golf tee goes in near the end of the outer word, not at its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A marketeer is a person who sells goods in a market, a kind of trader.

clue.text: Girl emerges from "the hell I endured"

indicators.note: something that emerges from a phrase comes out of it, sitting inside the words

blocks.note: the letters run across the words

explanation.surface: A young woman comes through a dreadful ordeal.
explanation.definitionFit: Ellie is a female first name, so a crossword can define it simply as a girl.

clue.text: Ran back at speed to report

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the word is read from its last letter

blocks.note: taken as written
a rate is a speed, as in rate of knots

explanation.surface: A messenger hurried back quickly to deliver news.
explanation.definitionFit: To narrate is to tell or give an account of events, which is to report them.

clue.text: Cola gets spy moving in WI-improvised song

indicators.note: letters that are moving shift out of place into a new order

blocks.note: letters to rearrange
letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A spy on a soft drink sets a song going.
explanation.walkthrough: WI is the abbreviation for the West Indies, home of this improvised musical style.
explanation.definitionFit: Calypso is a Caribbean song form, originally from Trinidad, often with improvised topical lyrics.

clue.text: English mint and nettle have spread, right?

indicators.note: plants that have spread grow out every which way, so the letters are scattered into a new order

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
letters to rearrange
letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A gardener notes that the herbs and weeds have run riot in an English garden.
explanation.definitionFit: An entitlement is a legal or moral claim to something, the same thing as a right.
